summary.text: For \(m=39101\), modular Lucas-sequence computations force \(2+\sqrt3\) to have order exactly \(N+1\) modulo any hypothetical least prime divisor \(q\) of \(N=201886\cdot3^{39101}-1\), using the prime factors \(2,3,100943\) of \(N+1\); this is impossible because the quadratic algebra has only \(q^2\le N\) elements, so \(N\) is prime. Hence a positive admissible exponent exists, and its least value cannot be zero.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the assertion by exhibiting a positive exponent, namely
\[
 m=39101,
\]
for which
\[
 2\cdot100943\cdot 3^m-1
\]
is prime.  Thus the set of positive exponents occurring in the definition of \(a(100943)\) is nonempty, so its least element cannot be zero.

The main issue is the primality proof for the 18,662-digit number
\[
 N=201886\cdot3^{39101}-1
   =2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1.
\]
We give the primality certificate and prove the criterion behind it.

1. The modular sequences used in the certificate

For an integer \(M\geq 3\), define
\[
 C_M(t)\equiv t(t^2-3)\pmod M,
 \qquad 0\leq C_M(t)<M.
\]
Starting from \(4\), put
\[
 Y_0=4,\qquad Y_{j+1}=C_N(Y_j).
\]
The certificate uses
\[
 y'=Y_{39100},\qquad y=Y_{39101}=C_N(y').
\]
This is an exact definition of the large residue \(y'\); no decimal expansion of its 18,661 digits is needed.

We also use Lucas sequences.  For a parameter \(T\) modulo \(N\), let
\[
 V_0(T)=2,\qquad V_1(T)=T,
\]
and
\[
 V_{r+2}(T)\equiv T V_{r+1}(T)-V_r(T)\pmod N.
\]
All representatives below are chosen in \(\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\).  Set
\[
 w=V_{100943}(y'),\qquad z=V_{100943}(y).
\]

For completeness, these Lucas residues can be calculated without running through all \(100943\) preceding terms.  If a pair \((A,B)\) represents \((V_k(T),V_{k+1}(T))\), the doubling identities are
\[
 V_{2k}=A^2-2,
 \qquad
 V_{2k+1}=AB-T,
 \qquad
 V_{2k+2}=B^2-2
 \pmod N.
\]
Consequently a binary ladder computes \(V_n(T)\): recursively compute the pair belonging to \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), and use the first two expressions when \(n\) is even and the last two when \(n\) is odd.  Since
\[
 100943<2^{17}=131072,
\]
17 binary stages suffice.

The finite certificate calculation gives the following four facts:
\[
 2^2\equiv 3\cdot1^2+1\pmod N,                                      \tag{1}
\]
\[
 z=N-2,                                                               \tag{2}
\]
\[
 \gcd\bigl((w^2-4)\bmod N,N\bigr)=1,                                 \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
 \gcd\bigl((y^2-4)\bmod N,N\bigr)=1.                                 \tag{4}
\]
Here \((x\bmod N)\) denotes the least nonnegative residue, so the expressions in (3) and (4) are unambiguous even if \(w^2-4\) or \(y^2-4\) is written using subtraction.

These are direct finite modular computations.  The long cubing chain was evaluated as four consecutive blocks of 9775 applications of \(C_N\), because
\[
 39100=4\cdot9775.
\]
The output of one block was used as the input to the next.  One further cubing gives \(y\).  The two Lucas values were then obtained by the 17-stage binary ladder just described.  Finally, Euclid’s algorithm gives the two gcds in (3) and (4).  Thus the role of the computation is precisely to establish the terminal Lucas congruence (2) and the two nonvanishing conditions (3) and (4).  Notice that (1) is simply the equality \(4=3+1\).

We now prove that these checks imply that \(N\) is prime.

2. Algebraic meaning of the recurrences

Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(N\) is composite, and let \(q\) be its least prime divisor.  Since \(m=39101\geq1\),
\[
 N+1=201886\cdot3^m.
\]
In particular, \(N\) is odd and \(N\equiv-1\equiv2\pmod3\).  Hence
\[
 q\neq2,\qquad q\neq3.                                                \tag{5}
\]
Because \(q\) is the least prime divisor of the composite number \(N\),
\[
 q^2\leq N.                                                           \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, writing \(N=qr\), if \(r<q\), then a prime divisor of \(r\) would be a prime divisor of \(N\) smaller than \(q\).

Work in the finite commutative ring
\[
 R=\mathbb F_q[\sqrt3]
   =\{a+b\sqrt3:a,b\in\mathbb F_q\},
\]
where multiplication is defined by
\[
 (a+b\sqrt3)(c+d\sqrt3)
  =(ac+3bd)+(ad+bc)\sqrt3.
\]
This ring has exactly \(q^2\) elements.  It need not be a field, but we need the following elementary reducedness property:
\[
 x^2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0.                                 \tag{7}
\]
To prove it, write \(x=a+b\sqrt3\).  The equation \(x^2=0\) says
\[
 a^2+3b^2=0,
 \qquad 2ab=0
\]
in \(\mathbb F_q\).  Since \(q\neq2\), the second equation gives \(a=0\) or \(b=0\).  If \(a=0\), then \(3b^2=0\), and since \(q\neq3\), we obtain \(b=0\).  If \(b=0\), then \(a^2=0\), so \(a=0\).  This proves (7).

Let
\[
 \beta=2+\sqrt3,
 \qquad
 \bar\beta=2-\sqrt3
\]
in \(R\).  From (1), or directly from \(4-3=1\),
\[
 \beta\bar\beta=1.                                                   \tag{8}
\]
Thus \(\beta\) and \(\bar\beta\) are inverse units.

The identity
\[
 (A+B)^3-3AB(A+B)=A^3+B^3
\]
shows why the cubing recurrence was chosen.  In view of (8), if a residue \(T\) represents \(A+B\), with \(AB=1\), then
\[
 C_N(T)\equiv T^3-3T\equiv A^3+B^3\pmod q,
\]
because \(q\mid N\).  Induction therefore gives
\[
 Y_j=\beta^{3^j}+\bar\beta^{3^j}\quad\text{in }R.                    \tag{9}
\]
In particular,
\[
 y'=\beta^{3^{m-1}}+\bar\beta^{3^{m-1}},                             \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
 y=\beta^{3^m}+\bar\beta^{3^m}.                                     \tag{11}
\]

More generally, whenever \(A B=1\) and \(T=A+B\), the Lucas recurrence gives
\[
 V_n(T)=A^n+B^n.                                                      \tag{12}
\]
This follows immediately by induction: it is true for \(n=0,1\), and
\[
 (A+B)(A^{n+1}+B^{n+1})-(A^n+B^n)
 =A^{n+2}+B^{n+2},
\]
using \(AB=1\).  Applying (12) to (10) and (11), and remembering that reduction modulo \(N\) may also be reduced modulo its divisor \(q\), gives
\[
 w=\beta^f+\bar\beta^f,
 \qquad f=3^{m-1}\cdot100943,                                       \tag{13}
\]
and
\[
 z=\beta^e+\bar\beta^e,
 \qquad e=3^m\cdot100943.                                           \tag{14}
\]
The relevant exponents satisfy
\[
 2e=N+1,                                                             \tag{15}
\]
\[
 3(2f)=N+1,                                                          \tag{16}
\]
and
\[
 100943(2\cdot3^m)=N+1.                                              \tag{17}
\]

3. Determining the order of \(\beta\)

Condition (2), reduced modulo \(q\), says that \(z=-2\) in \(R\).  By (14),
\[
 \beta^e+\bar\beta^e=-2.
\]
Also, by (8),
\[
 \beta^e\bar\beta^e=1.
\]
Let \(x=\beta^e\).  Then \(\bar\beta^e=x^{-1}\), and the two displayed equations imply
\[
 (x+1)^2=x(x+x^{-1}+2)=0.
\]
By the reducedness property (7), \(x+1=0\).  Hence
\[
 \beta^e=-1.                                                         \tag{18}
\]
Using (15), we obtain
\[
 \beta^{N+1}=\beta^{2e}=1.                                          \tag{19}
\]
Moreover \(\beta^e\neq1\), because \(q\neq2\), so \(-1\neq1\) in \(R\).

We next prove
\[
 \beta^{2f}\neq1.                                                    \tag{20}
\]
Suppose instead that \(\beta^{2f}=1\).  Since \(\bar\beta=\beta^{-1}\), this also gives \(\bar\beta^{2f}=1\).  Put
\[
 r=\beta^f,\qquad s=\bar\beta^f.
\]
Then \(rs=1\), \(r^2=s^2=1\), and by (13), \(w=r+s\) in \(R\).  Therefore
\[
 w^2-4=(r+s)^2-4=r^2+s^2+2rs-4=1+1+2-4=0
\]
in \(R\), and in particular in its first coordinate \(\mathbb F_q\).  Thus \(q\) divides the integer residue \((w^2-4)\bmod N\).  Since \(q\mid N\), it follows that \(q\) divides
\[
 \gcd\bigl((w^2-4)\bmod N,N\bigr),
\]
contradicting (3), because a prime \(q>1\) cannot divide 1.  This proves (20).

Similarly, we claim
\[
 \beta^{2\cdot3^m}\neq1.                                            \tag{21}
\]
If equality held, it would also hold for \(\bar\beta\).  Set
\[
 r=\beta^{3^m},\qquad s=\bar\beta^{3^m}.
\]
Then again \(rs=1\), \(r^2=s^2=1\), while (11) gives \(y=r+s\).  Hence \(y^2-4=0\) in \(R\).  As above, \(q\) would divide both \((y^2-4)\bmod N\) and \(N\), contrary to (4).  This proves (21).

We now show that the multiplicative order of \(\beta\) is exactly \(N+1\).  Equation (19) shows that the order divides \(N+1\).  The prime factorization relevant here is
\[
 N+1=201886\cdot3^m=2\cdot100943\cdot3^m.                            \tag{22}
\]
The integer \(100943\) is prime.  For example, trial division by the primes at most \(317\) gives no divisor, and
\[
 317^2<100943<318^2;
\]
every composite integer has a prime divisor not exceeding its square root.  Thus the only prime divisors of \(N+1\) are
\[
 2,\quad3,\quad100943.                                               \tag{23}
\]

For each of these primes, \(\beta^{(N+1)/p}\neq1\):

* For \(p=2\), \((N+1)/2=e\), and (18) gives \(\beta^e=-1\neq1\).

* For \(p=3\), equation (16) gives \((N+1)/3=2f\), and nonvanishing is (20).

* For \(p=100943\), equation (17) gives
  \((N+1)/100943=2\cdot3^m\), and nonvanishing is (21).

A standard elementary order argument now yields
\[
 \operatorname{ord}(\beta)=N+1.                                     \tag{24}
\]
Indeed, if its order \(d\) were a proper divisor of \(N+1\), then \((N+1)/d>1\) would have a prime divisor \(p\).  This \(p\) would divide \(N+1\), and \(d\mid(N+1)/p\), forcing \(\beta^{(N+1)/p}=1\), contrary to the corresponding case above.

But \(R\) has only \(q^2\) elements.  The distinct powers
\[
 1,\beta,\ldots,\beta^{\operatorname{ord}(\beta)-1}
\]
are elements of \(R\), so
\[
 \operatorname{ord}(\beta)\leq q^2.
\]
Together with (24) and (6), this gives
\[
 N+1\leq q^2\leq N,
\]
an impossibility.  Therefore the supposition that \(N\) was composite is false, and
\[
 201886\cdot3^{39101}-1

a prime.                                                             \tag{25}
\]

4. Disproof of the proposed sequence value

For \(n=100943\), let
\[
 S=\{r\in\mathbb N:r>0\text{ and }2\cdot100943\cdot3^r-1
       \text{ is prime}\}.
\]
Because \(201886=2\cdot100943\), statement (25) says exactly that
\[
 39101\in S.
\]
Thus \(S\) is nonempty.  By definition, \(a(100943)\) is the least member of \(S\) (with value zero only in the no-prime case).  Every member of \(S\) is strictly positive, so its least member is also strictly positive.  In particular,
\[
 a(100943)\neq0.
\]
This contradicts, and therefore disproves, the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\).  The argument does not need to assert that 39101 is the least successful exponent; its primality already suffices to show that the value is not zero.
